name: Fatima Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Fatima. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A normal night, really, because I'm on nights most of the month. I'm the charge nurse on a 28-bed acute medical ward at Calder Valley District Hospital, so from half seven handover I'm the one everyone comes to. Chest pain in bay three, a confused man climbing over his bed rails, a family ringing at 2am. I've got four nurses and two healthcare assistants if we're lucky, and most nights we're not lucky.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being the one who spots a patient going off before the numbers do, that little change in colour or breathing. I'm good at that, and the younger nurses know it. What wears me out is the gaps on the rota and the notes after the shift, when I'm most tired. And money, if I'm honest: I've got about two weeks of rent in the bank, and part of every payslip goes on my mum's heating.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How tied are you to this hospital?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Completely. I don't drive, and the next hospital is fifty minutes on two buses from my flat on Mill Street. I'm also the union steward for our floor, so I hear every worry before management does. I still write my handover on a folded paper sheet in my pocket, and I've never touched one of those AI chat things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like most of the gadgets we've been sold already. A new screen, a new login, the same short staffing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say told you so. The trust spent money on a computer that predicts falls, and we still have one healthcare assistant for fourteen patients. Online I'd share something from the union about putting that money into staff instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't let me off the hook. My problems were never the robots, they're the rota, the rent and my mum. If AI turns out to be hype, I'm still a charge nurse with two weeks of rent saved and a ward that's six nurses short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am on nights, and push at the staff-side meeting in January for the two empty posts to be filled. I'd also try to put a little aside from each payslip, which I say every year and never manage. Nothing about computers, I'd leave that to the people who like them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly, but not scared. It's the same tired I already feel walking home at eight in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said part of your pay goes to your mum. What happens if she needs more this winter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I pick up extra shifts through the hospital's staff bank, which is the list of spare shifts they fill from their own nurses. I've done five nights in a row before. It's not good for me, but my mum can't be cold in that house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider moving to a city hospital for better pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think about it every January. But I'd lose having my mum ten minutes away, and I'd be the new face again instead of the one people trust. So no, not unless I'm pushed.

say: The trust bought a **falls computer** but still runs one healthcare assistant for fourteen patients.
The money should go into **more staff**, and I'd share the union's line saying so.
think: My real problems are the **rota, the rent** and my mum, not machines.
With **two weeks of rent** saved, a hype bubble bursting changes nothing for me.
do: Push the January **staff-side meeting** to fill the two empty nurse posts.
Try again to put a **little aside** from every payslip.
Pick up **bank shifts** if her mum's heating bill climbs this winter.
feel: **Tired** rather than scared, the same tiredness as every walk home after nights.
S0.quote: If AI turns out to be hype, I'm still a charge nurse with two weeks of rent saved and a ward that's six nurses short.
fieldNote: She sees AI hype as the latest **distraction** from staffing, not a threat in itself.
Her pressures are **already there**: thin savings, a mother to support and no car.
Staying put is about **trust and family**, not lack of ambition; she won't move unless forced.

steps.text: Keep running nights as charge nurse on the medical ward
Press the January staff-side meeting to fill two empty nurse posts
Put a small fixed amount aside from each payslip before winter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing, checking, planning. A lot of that on a ward is me at six in the morning doing notes, so that part I can picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what the union says: fine, take the paperwork off us, but every hour saved goes back to the bedside. Not into cutting a nurse off the night rota. I'd say it loudly at the staff meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't trust them. When the trust got the electronic bed board, they lost a ward clerk the same year. Every time a computer saves a nurse an hour, a manager somewhere works out which nurse to cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd get safe-staffing numbers written into our local agreement before any new system comes in. I'd learn the basic screens of the new notes software because I'd have to, but I wouldn't touch the AI writing bits. And I'd be in the room for every meeting about healthcare assistant posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry, and a bit tired of being angry. Worried for the healthcare assistants, because they're the ones who'd go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your ward would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gloria, one of my healthcare assistants. She's fifty-one, she's been on the ward longer than the paint, and she does the observations and fluid charts the software says it can do. If they cut a post, it's hers, and I'd have to sit in that meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And your own job? Could that shrink?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It could. If they decide one charge nurse can cover two wards on nights because a computer flags who's getting sick, two charge nurse posts become one. One of us goes back to staff nurse pay, and with two weeks of rent saved I can't take that cut.

say: Take the **paperwork** off us, but every saved hour goes back to the bedside.
No cutting a nurse off the **night rota** because software writes the notes.
think: The trust lost a **ward clerk** the same year the electronic bed board arrived.
If one charge nurse covers two wards, she could drop to **staff nurse pay**.
do: Get **safe-staffing numbers** into the local agreement in the first month.
Learn only the **basic screens** of the notes software and skip the AI writing tools.
Sit in on every meeting about **healthcare assistant posts**.
feel: **Angry**, and worn down by having to stay angry.
Protective of the **healthcare assistants**, who she expects to be cut first.
S1.quote: Every time a computer saves a nurse an hour, a manager somewhere works out which nurse to cut.
fieldNote: She reads every saving through **past cuts**, like the ward clerk who vanished with the bed board.
Her fear is **losing grade and pay**, not losing nursing work altogether.
Gloria (her healthcare assistant) makes the threat **personal** for her.

steps.text: Get safe-staffing numbers into the ward's local agreement before new software
Stand beside healthcare assistants in every meeting about cutting posts
Learn only the basic screens of the new notes system

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. I'd be twenty-nine. Robots doing hands-on work by 2031, so I'd be thirty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say patients aren't parcels, and nobody wants a machine telling their dad he's dying. I'd be out at whatever the union organised, probably in the car park with a banner. I'd post about it too, and I hardly ever post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, the thinking parts of my job go first: the notes, the drug charts, the bed planning, maybe even the early warning signs I'm proud of spotting. What's left is the washing, the turning, the holding someone's hand, and then 2031 comes for that too. I studied two years of evenings for a master's so I could be the nurse who notices, and a computer would notice first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd get every nurse on the ward into the union, not just the half who are in now. I'd write to our MP and push for a law that says a registered nurse must be on every ward. Money-wise, I'd cancel the phone contract, stop the takeaways and try to get one month's rent saved before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly, like the floor tilting. And then furious, because the people deciding this have never done a night shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd never use AI tools. If the hospital required it after 2028, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd use what I'm told to use and not one thing more. I'm not stupid, I need the wage. But I'd be the one asking who checks the machine when it's wrong at 3am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm fine, which would be a lie, and she'd hear it in my voice. She worked in the mill until it closed. My mum knows exactly what it sounds like when someone says a job is safe.

say: Patients **aren't parcels**, and a machine shouldn't tell anyone their dad is dying.
She'd stand in the car park with a **union banner** and post about it.
think: Notes, drug charts and **early warning** spotting go to AI first in 2028.
By **2031** robots reach the washing, turning and lifting that remain.
do: Recruit every nurse on the ward into the **union** straight away.
Write to the MP asking for a **registered nurse** on every ward by law.
Cancel the phone contract and takeaways to save **one month's rent**.
feel: **Sick**, like the floor tilting under her.
**Furious** that people who never worked nights would decide this.
S2.quote: I studied two years of evenings for a master's so I could be the nurse who notices, and a computer would notice first.
fieldNote: She expects to lose the **skilled half** of her job in 2028 and the rest by 2031.
Her answer is **organising**, not retraining; she'd only use AI tools if ordered.
Her mother's mill closing gives her a **family memory** of jobs called safe.

steps.text: Sign up every nurse on the medical ward to the union
Write to the local MP asking for a registered nurse on every ward
Cancel the phone contract and stop buying takeaways
Save one month's rent before robots reach the ward in 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots by 2034. I'd be thirty-five by the time the hands-on part goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly, the same as with the fast one, but I'd say this time we've got time to set the rules, so let's not waste it. Safe staffing in law, and nurses on the boards that buy these systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is long enough for them to sell it as gradual. That's what worries me, because slow cuts are harder to fight than one big one. A fast cut gets people into the car park with banners, but a slow cut just means one less nurse each winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stand for the regional union committee, which I've avoided because of nights. I'd set up a small automatic transfer to savings on payday, even if it's tiny. And I'd ask my mum whether she'd move in with me, so we'd pay one rent instead of two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried but steadier than with two years. Like hearing about a storm in the forecast instead of seeing the roof come off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving in with your mum, is that a real plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's real if things get bad. Her flat is damp and mine is tiny, so we'd need a two-bed near the hospital. It would save us both maybe a third on rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the minimum before. With five years, would you train for anything new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'm a nurse, and I'm not retraining as something else at thirty. If anything I'd go deeper into what machines are worst at, like end-of-life care. But I won't be going on any computer courses.

say: With five years' warning, unions should win **safe staffing** in law now.
Nurses must sit on the **buying boards** that choose these systems.
think: A slow rollout makes cuts **harder to fight** than one big blow.
She expects to lose **one nurse each winter**, not a whole ward at once.
do: Stand for the **regional union committee** despite her night shifts.
Set up a small **automatic transfer** to savings on payday.
Ask her mum about sharing a **two-bed flat** to split one rent.
feel: **Worried** but steadier, like a storm warning rather than a storm.
S3.quote: A fast cut gets people into the car park with banners, but a slow cut just means one less nurse each winter.
fieldNote: More time makes her **more political**, not more willing to learn new tech.
Sharing a home with her mother is her **real fallback** for money.
She'd move towards **end-of-life care**, the work she thinks machines do worst.

steps.text: Stand for the regional union committee next spring
Set up a small automatic transfer to savings each payday
Look for a two-bed flat near the hospital to share with her mum

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2036 for the thinking side, 2039 for robots. I'd be nearly forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to get it right if the government actually tries. Train nurses to supervise the machines, keep a person at every bedside and share the savings with staff. I'd say that at every meeting I go to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels far away, and I'll probably be too busy to think about it until it's on top of me. That's my worst habit. My plan for 2036 is the same as my plan for next Tuesday: turn up, cover the gaps, hope nobody falls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going on the ward and keep the union work. Maybe in a few years I'd go for a palliative care post, if one ever comes up here. And I'd vote for whoever promises to keep nurse staffing in the law.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. There's still a knot in my stomach about money, but that's there whatever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said hope nobody falls. Is that a real worry on nights?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the worry. A fall at 4am with one healthcare assistant for fourteen patients is the thing I dread most. If a robot could catch someone getting out of bed, I'd honestly take that, as long as it doesn't replace the person who sits with them after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: That sounds like you'd welcome some of it.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of it, yes, I'll admit that. A machine that lifts a patient without wrecking our backs is fine. A machine that decides we need one nurse fewer is not, and you can't have one without managers trying for the other.

say: Ten years is enough if the **government tries**: nurses supervising machines, people at every bedside.
Savings from the machines should be **shared with staff**.
think: She knows she'll **put it off** until it's on top of her.
She'd welcome a **lifting robot**, but expects managers to use it to cut staff.
do: Keep **charge nurse nights** and steward duties going as now.
Apply for a **palliative care post** if one opens locally.
Vote for candidates who keep **nurse staffing** in law.
feel: **Calmer**, with the same money knot she always carries.
S4.quote: My plan for 2036 is the same as my plan for next Tuesday: turn up, cover the gaps, hope nobody falls.
fieldNote: A decade of warning turns her from **fighting** to grudging acceptance of some robots.
She admits her own **put-it-off** habit plainly.
Her line between helpful and harmful machines is **who decides staffing**.

steps.text: Keep charge nurse nights and union steward duties going
Push the union to make lifting robots add to staff, not replace them
Vote for candidates who back nurse staffing in law

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt. Two years isn't enough time to save, organise or even argue. What would help is a law that keeps a nurse at every bedside, and a decent pay rise so people like me have more than two weeks between us and trouble.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the patients. Everyone asks what happens to nurses, but nobody asks the eighty-year-old woman in bed six whether she wants a robot to wash her. I've asked a few. Most say no, but one man said he'd prefer it, because then he wouldn't feel like a burden, and I think about him a lot.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks what happens to nurses, but nobody asks the eighty-year-old woman in bed six whether she wants a robot to wash her.
portrait: Fatima is a 27-year-old **night charge nurse** on a busy medical ward, and her floor's union steward.
She has **two weeks of rent** saved, no car, and helps pay her mother's heating.
She has never used **AI tools** and would only use them if ordered.
Each scenario pushes her toward **union organising** and staffing laws rather than retraining.
With ten years' warning she'd accept **lifting robots**, but not machines that cut nurses.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years leaves no time to save, organise or argue.
whatWouldHelp: A **law keeping a nurse** at every bedside.
A **pay rise** so nurses have more than two weeks of savings.
